content: When performing aerosol-generating procedures on suspected cases, implement strict airborne precautions to prevent transmission. Healthcare workers should be monitored for symptoms such as fever and influenza-like illness to ensure early detection of potential infections. Provide healthcare workers with appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) and ensure they receive adequate training on its proper use. Cases should be managed meticulously to prevent progression to severe illness or death. Oseltamivir should be administered as the primary antiviral treatment, following the standard regimen used for seasonal influenza virus infections. In certain cases, modified regimens of oseltamivir treatment, such as higher dosages, extended duration, or combination therapy with amantadine or rimantadine, may be considered based on individual patient needs. If there is an insufficient national supply of oseltamivir, the World Health Organization (WHO) can provide it from its strategic global stockpile. Corticosteroids should not be used routinely but may be considered in cases of septic shock with suspected adrenal insufficiency. Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis is not recommended. However, if pneumonia is present, initial antibiotic treatment for community-acquired pneumonia is appropriate and should subsequently be guided by microbiological findings. Oxygen saturation should be monitored whenever possible, and supplemental oxygen should be provided to correct hypoxemia. For acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) associated with the A(H5N1) virus, therapy should follow published, evidence-based guidelines for sepsis-associated ARDS, including lung-protective mechanical ventilation strategies. Laboratory-confirmed cases must be reported to WHO under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005). To gather more information on treatment and outcomes, a clinical data reporting form is available, and treating physicians should be encouraged to complete and return it to WHO. Vaccinations for Humans Influenza A(H5N1) vaccines are not widely available, and their use would depend on the assessed risk of infection. Individuals with occupational exposure to A(H5N1) should be vaccinated with seasonal influenza vaccines to reduce the risk of reassortment between human and avian influenza viruses. WHO does not maintain a stockpile of A(H5N1) vaccines. Seasonal influenza vaccination is recommended for healthcare workers in all countries to protect their patients from seasonal influenza infections. In countries affected by influenza A(H5N1), vaccination against seasonal influenza is recommended for groups at increased risk of exposure to the avian influenza virus as a measure to reduce the likelihood of simultaneous infection with avian and human influenza viruses. This reduces the risk of reassortment and the emergence of a novel influenza virus with pandemic potential. It is important to note that current seasonal influenza vaccines derived from circulating human influenza viruses do not provide protection against human infection with avian influenza A viruses. Vaccines for the A(H5N1) virus have been developed based on WHO-recommended candidate vaccine viruses and are licensed in several countries. However, they are not widely available, and their use would depend on the assessed risk of infection. Some countries are stockpiling these vaccines as part of their pandemic preparedness measures. Vaccination is recommended for first responders to human or animal A(H5N1) outbreaks and for healthcare workers managing suspected or confirmed A(H5N1) cases in designated referral facilities. Vaccination is not recommended for individuals who may only potentially come into contact with infected animals, essential workers in areas where A(H5N1) is enzootic, or the general population. Pandemic Vaccine It is currently impossible to predict which influenza virus type will cause the next pandemic. As a result, the production of a pandemic influenza vaccine can only begin once the pandemic influenza virus has been identified. Given the current influenza vaccine technology used by most manufacturers, the first doses of a pandemic vaccine would only become available within four to six months after the identification of the pandemic influenza virus. This document compiles information from WHO, FAO, and other UN agencies, as well as the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), on recommendations and guidelines related to avian influenza. It is intended to assist WHO country offices and national institutions in advising Member States on human health concerns arising from avian influenza outbreaks in animals or suspected human infections. As new information becomes available, this document will be reviewed and updated accordingly.
